o1.biggest_strength: It answers the 20% question with the lifetime maths, keeps the top 20 at the centre, and turns the 30-day credit window and payout complaints into concrete fixes the one manager can run.
o1.biggest_mistake: The $38,000 'saving on new customers only' is a rough assumption and is flagged as needing checking, so finance may challenge that line.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Tighten the new-customer saving estimate to one number finance can stand behind, or drop it and lean on the break-even and churn maths.

o2.biggest_strength: Clear, plain-English case for holding 30% and a well-explained 90-day window, with a Partner tier that rewards the top 20 and a first 30 days anyone could run.
o2.biggest_mistake: The 40% for 12 months to Partners is a real cost and a divergence from the 'one rate, no menu' simplicity; the $63,000 per 10% credited-revenue estimate is loose and the break-even claim ($262,500) is right but the 'four people wipe it out' logic is hand-wavy.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Drop or clearly price the 40% Partner headline (or show why it beats the simpler same-rate tier), and tighten the credited-revenue cost estimate to a defensible range.

reason: Both get the big calls right, but Output 1 is the cleaner single plan: same rate, no menu, sharper step-by-step first 30 days and a short review trigger. Output 2's 40% Partner headline adds cost and complexity without the survey or churn data demanding it.
